author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Farmers, fisherfolk demand urgent aid amid El Niño, rising fuel prices
content:
The absence of reliable irrigation makes it difficult for farmers to continue planting during periods of extreme heat.







By Wendyl Geronimo

Davao Today




From drought-stricken farms in Davao and Nueva Ecija to fishing communities in Albay, farmers and fisherfolk are demanding government assistance, protection against land grabbing and genuine agrarian reform as El Niño, mounting production costs and development projects threaten their livelihoods.




Amid worsening agricultural conditions, rising production expenses and continuing disputes over land ownership, farmers and fisherfolk across the Philippines are calling for immediate government intervention, warning that insufficient assistance and threats of displacement are pushing rural communities deeper into poverty.




Their demands come as agricultural communities confront the effects of El Niño, inadequate irrigation systems, expensive fuel and fertilizer, and development projects that farmers organizations say threaten thousands of hectares of farmland.




In the Davao Region, prolonged dry conditions have affected agricultural production, particularly among farmers dependent on rainfall.




Approximately P410 million in agricultural losses were recorded in the Davao region due to El Niño.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Farmers reiterate demand for genuine agrarian reform
content:
MANILA — Farmers, fisherfolk along with Indigenous peoples and advocates culminated this year’s Peasant Month on October 21 by marching from España to Mendiola after a week-long camp out, bringing longstanding calls for genuine agrarian reform.

The Super El Niño, land-use conversion and human rights abuses are among the key issues aggravating the plight of rural folk.

Farmers from Southern Tagalog and Central Luzon expressed deep frustration by the state’s suggestion to use buckets to collect water. They decried the lack of government aid like subsidies for the dry spells, leaving many without food to sustain themselves and their families.

Other issues they highlighted are the Pax Silica initiative and various renewable energy projects which will convert their farmland into infrastructure which they said “will serve corporate interests and the US military complex.”

They condemned the continuing U.S. intervention in many aspects of the nation’s affairs. They vowed to hold protest actions on the upcoming visit of U.S. President Donald Trump,or this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) forum. (RVO)

Text and photos by Viggo Sarmago

author: Danilo Arao
title: Pulis
content:
Policemen disperse the protesters in front of the House of Representatives, Sept. 9. (Photo by Jose Santos)

Walang maaasahan sa institusyong hindi nagsisilbi sa interes ng mga nasa laylayan.

Insulto man sa halaman at hayop na hindi hamak na mas may ambag sa pananatili ng kalikasan, naging uso na ang mga terminong pulis patola at pulis buwaya para ilarawan ang kabulukan at kapalpakan ng institusyong dapat na nagsisilbi at nagtatanggol sa mamamayan.

May mga nakaunipormeng wagas kung magpahayag ng kanilang karahasan. Pati mapayapang protesta, pinipigilan. Sinusugod ang barikada. Nang-aaresto nang walang pakundangan. Nanunulak at namamalo ng mga dumadalo sa rally. Walang pakialam kung may humandusay sa kalyeng duguan. Mistulang nawala na ang katinuan dahil sa pagiging utak pulbura.

Sadyang walang pakialam, walang paggalang sa batayang karapatan. Kahit ang mga peryodista, hindi na ligtas sa kalupitan ng pulis. Noong Okt. 19, may peryodistang sinaktan dahil lang nagkober ng protesta ng mga magsasaka sa tapat ng gusali ng Department of Agrarian Reform.

Sinubukan pa siyang arestuhin. Napilitan lang siyang pakawalan dahil napansing maraming nagbibidyo ng nangyari at maraming aktibistang lumalapit para ipaliwanag na peryodista ang kinakaladkad at pinagtutulungan nila.

Nakapagtataka lang na binabaligtad ngayon ng mga pulis ang nangyari. “Initial reports indicate that a verbal altercation occurred involving an individual who identified himself as a member of the media and deployed police personnel. The individual allegedly uttered profane remarks and kicked several police personnel. In response, the officers intervened to prevent further escalation. The individual was subsequently released.”

Kung susuriin ang press release ng mga pulis noong Okt. 20, hindi binanggit na iniwan nilang sugatan ang peryodistang pinagtulungang damputin at kaladkarin. Tila hindi nangyari ang ilang beses na pagsigaw niya ng “Media ako!” habang ipinapakita ang press ID na hindi pinansin ng mga nagbibingi-bingihan at nagbubulag-bulagan.

Basta para sa kanila, may kailangang masampolan para hindi na siya gayahin ng iba pang peryodista. Kahit na hindi nila binanggit ang terminong “chilling effect,” ito pa rin ang nais nilang mangyari para mapatahimik ang midya sa pag-uulat ng mga nangyayari sa lipunan, lalo na sa kanayunan.

Kinikilala at nirerespeto raw ng mga pulis ang kalayaan sa pamamahayag, pati na ang tinatawag nilang “peaceful assembly.” Pero bakit parati silang humihingi ng “permit to rally” para magkaroon ng mga mapayapang pagtitipon? Gayundin ang nangyari sa pagkilos ng mga magsasaka kamakailan. Pinapadaan sa komplikadong burukrasya ang lehitimong pagpapahayag ng saloobin.

Hanggang ngayon, ginagamit pa ring batayan ng represyon ang Batas Pambansa 880 o Public Assembly Act of 1985 na ipinatupad ng diktador na si Ferdinand Marcos Sr. Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napapanahon nang ibasura ang batas na itong sinisikil ang batayang karapatan. Kung totoong naglilingkod sa interes ng mamamayan ang mga pulis, dapat na hinahayaan lang nila ang mga mapayapang pagtitipon at hindi nila pagmamalupitan ang mga nagpoprotesta’t peryodista.

Pero walang maaasahan sa institusyong hindi nagsisilbi sa interes ng mga nasa laylayan. Palibhasa, mas pinapaboran nila ang interes ng mga nasa kapangyarihan. Sadyang may kabulukang nagreresulta sa utak pulburang oryentasyon. Asahang patuloy na lalabanan ang kanilang pandarahas sa mga peryodista’t ordinaryong mamamayan.

Patola na, buwaya pa. Idagdag na rin ang mga salitang marahas at sinungaling. Posible ring tawagin silang kaaway ng kapayapaan. Sa konteksto ng pagpapatuloy ng kanilang masamang gawi, mainam na isang salita na lang ang gamitin. Pasista.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Southern Tagalog workers on 45-peso wage hike: ‘Insulting’
content:
The workers reiterated their demand for a P1,200 (US$18.92) national minimum wage.

CABUYAO CITY — Workers in Southern Tagalog denounced the newly approved wage increase of P25 (US$0.39) to P45 (US$0.71) for minimum wage earners, saying the adjustment offers little relief to workers struggling with rising prices of food, fuel, and other basic necessities.

The Alyansa ng mga Manggagawa sa Probinsya ng Laguna (ALMAPILA) and Pagkakaisa ng mga Manggagawa sa Timog Katagalugan – Kilusang Mayo Uno (PAMANTIK-KMU) described the wage adjustment as an insult to workers in Laguna and the rest of Southern Tagalog.

In a protest October 16 outside the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) IV-A office, the Workers’ Initiative for Wage Increase-Southern Tagalog (WIN4WIN-ST) criticized Wage Order No. 23 as insufficient to address the widening gap between wages and the cost of living.

“Workers in CALABARZON have long endured extremely low wages, cutting back on expenses, pawning their ATM cards, getting sick, and going hungry despite their significant contribution to the national economy,” WIN4WIN-ST said in a statement.

The groups argued that even as workers’ nominal wages increase, their purchasing power remains under pressure from the rising cost of basic goods and services.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: ‘Release tortured Mangyan organizer’
content:
“He needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.”

Indigenous Mangyan farmer and organizer Miguel Magbata was reportedly beaten and tortured while in military custody after his arrest in Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro, on October 14, prompting human rights groups to call for his immediate release and to hold accountable those responsible.

According to Karapatan Southern Tagalog, Magbata was arrested after a reported armed encounter between the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and alleged New People’s Army (NPA) members in Sitio Badyang, Barangay San Roque in Bulalacao. He was reportedly subjected to physical abuse and interrogation by the 1st Infantry Battalion (IB) under the command of the 203rd Infantry Brigade (IBde).

After days of uncertainty over his whereabouts, reports emerged that Magbata was transferred to Roxas Municipal Police Station. Defend Mindoro said that he needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.

The group also raised concerns over a Facebook post from 203rd Infantry Brigade of Philippine Army about Magbata’s children and family, published without their consent, which it said could compromise their safety.

Despite his reported transfer to police custody, the military reportedly sought to retain custody of Magbata. Defend Mindoro demanded his immediate release and called for accountability from the 203rd IBde led by Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo, and the 1st IB, under Lt. Col. Edwin Mirador.

Defend Mindoro said that Magbata’s case shows a pattern of harassment and abuses against Indigenous Peoples, farmers, and community organizers in Mindoro where those asserting their rights are often accused of links to the communist armed movement.

The group cited the killings of Indigenous and peasant individuals Jay-el Maligday, Hulyo Agtay, and Juan Sumilhig which it attributed to military abuses. It also stressed the case of Dolores Solangon, an elderly Mangyan-Iraya woman who reportedly endured illegal arrest and nine hours of torture at the hands of elements from the 76th IB.

Maligday, a young Hanunuo-Mangyan, was allegedly killed by soldiers of the 4th IB while sleeping in his home. The same unit was accused of beating another Hanunuo-Mangyan, Minggo, in Mansalay early this year.

For Defend Mindoro, these abuses are inseparable from the land disputes and economic hardships confronting Indigenous communities and farmers.

In Bulalacao, the group said that large-scale mining and renewable energy projects threaten ancestral lands and local livelihoods. These include developments associated with CleanTech Global Renewables and Singapore-based The Blue Circle which is reportedly planning an offshore wind project involving 100 turbines across a proposed 40,050-hectare area.

Meanwhile, drought has exacerbated the farmers’ hardship. In 2024, an estimated 864 hectares of farmland in Bulalacao were damaged, resulting in P87 million (US$1.37 million) in agricultural losses and affecting around 1,000 registered farmers, according to Defend Mindoro. With another severe El Niño episode looming, communities face renewed threats of crop failure and water shortage.

The group criticized the government for prioritizing counterinsurgency operations over addressing rural poverty, landlessness, and the climate crisis. It said that militarization further endangers communities already struggling to protect their livelihoods and ancestral territories.

Defend Mindoro demanded an independent investigation into the allegations of torture and illegal detention. Torture is prohibited under international law and civilians must be protected from violence and cruel treatment in situations of armed conflict.

The group held the 203rd IBde and the Marcos Jr. administration accountable for the alleged violations, calling for an end to military harassment of Indigenous Peoples and farmers.

For Defend Mindoro, Magbata’s case underscores the dangers faced by community organizers defending the rights of rural communities. “No allegation of insurgency can justify torture or the denial of due process,” the group wrote in a statement. (DAA)

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Farmers decry government’s lack of preparation for Super El Niño
content:
Farmers, scientists and environmentalists, held a forum, October 18 on the impacts of Super El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk and the government’s lack of preparations for it.

A Super El Niño is a stronger El Niño where the temperature of the Pacific Ocean increases to 2C above the average. In the Philippines, it leads to the extreme shifting of weather conditions, bringing in severe drought, or stronger rainfall events. For farmers, it is the government’s unpreparedness that turns it into an even greater calamity, made even worse by the climate crisis.

Farmers Geraldine Patriarca and Ginny Nabia from Bicol and Negros expressed how their communities are already experiencing extreme drought, and are unable to sustain themselves and their families. They demanded Marcos Jr. to give genuine solutions to farmers’ struggles, not his proposed buckets that they say “will barely even catch any rain.”

Irish Cuaresma of Advocates of Science and Technology for the People (Agham), added that farmers and Indigenous peoples are further undermined by “disaster capitalism,” where corporations benefit from humanitarian crises.

Sharl Lopez of Philippine Network of Food Security Programs (PNFSP) meanwhile, criticized the government for not upholding their obligation to uphold the people’s right to food security, and advocated for the passing of the Right to Adequate Food Bill.

author: Anne Marxze Umil
title: Int’l solidarity vs Pax Silica
content:
At the Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder workshop in Bangkok, Thailand on October 14, 2026. (Photo from ILPS Philippines Facebook page)

Despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance.

BANGKOK – Organizations from different parts of the world are now united against the Pax Silica Initiative to be signed by the United States and the Philippines in November. US President Donald Trump reportedly will visit the Philippines to sign the agreement.

“We are in a period of extreme conflict between two very powerful and imperialist countries and the US is trembling and shaking. We have to maintain that fervor of revolution, that ability to throw stones at them, to bring them down and to make sure that the US imperialist power is no more,” said Azra Sayeed, secretary-general of the International League of Peoples Struggles (ILPS) during an activity in Bangkok, Thailand dubbed “Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder” on October 14.

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank (IMF-WB) held its annual meeting in Bangkok from October 12 to 18. Participants included central bank governors, economic policy makers and business leaders.

In a statement, the Campaigners of the Peoples Global Campaign (PGC) Against IMF and World expressed concern over IMF-WB’s push for new technologies, including the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Global South economies.

The group said that the “frantic race” for AI dominance intensified mining and extraction in resource-rich countries in the Global South. Transnational corporations are extracting rare earth elements (REEs) and other critical minerals to meet the growing demand for AI infrastructure. To secure control over the AI supply chain, countries like the US initiated the formation of Pax Silica and other similar formations.

“We know that imperialism is about world domination and control over resources. In the previous century, the rivalry among imperialist powers centered on oil because whoever controlled oil could wield significant influence over the military and the economy,” Arnold Padilla, secretary-general of ILPS-Philippines said during the event.

Now, he stressed, the battle is over critical minerals as whoever controls AI and the critical minerals needed to build its infrastructure could gain a significant advantage in dominating the world. “Essentially, that’s the battle now between the US and China. So, who will control this critical sector?”

This is why, Padilla said, the Philippines is up for a major battle to halt the signing of the US-led Pax Silica Initiative this year in time for the Asean Summit from November 16 to 18.

He said that AI is not just about the software that people use but also about weapons like drones “that can make decisions in actual battles without any human intervention.” He added that these sophisticated weapons will be made of minerals to be extracted from the Philippines.

Read: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica? Read: War and plunder: US imperialism in the Philippines

“Pax Silica is made up of 24 countries, of course, led by the US. And it’s a special coalition. Specifically chosen by the US because countries that belong to Pax Silica perform a specific specialized role because it’s about controlling the supply chain,” Padilla said. “We don’t have high technology, we don’t have the logistic network, we don’t have capital or energy. But what do we have? We have the critical minerals. So for us in the Philippines, this is all about plunder.”

Donna Denina, secretary-general of International Women’s Alliance (IWA), said that US Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, former tech executive and adviser tied to the controversial software firm Palantir, designed Pax Silica to give the US control over the global technology supply chain.

Palantir is a technology firm with clients from the Pentagon and foreign militaries including the Israeli government. But Denina said that Palantir is now expanding its influence beyond military tech into the health care sector.

In the US, she said that Palantir’s AI software is being used to manage hospital staffing and scheduling. This raised concerns among healthcare workers and prompted protests.

She said that more than 1,000 nurses from the National Nurses United union protested against healthcare institutions’ contracts with Palantir. “They are concerned that AI systems could replace human decision-making in the hospital. Nurses warn that relying on AI could reduce human oversight in decisions affecting patients’ care and well-being.”

She stressed that Palantir’s expansion in the United Kingdom’s National Health Service (NHS) was also protested by patients, health workers and the public.

Denina said that with the expansion of AI requires large data centers that consume vast amounts of land and water. She said that this is why some US states and cities banned or restricted the construction of data centers.

According to Data Center Watch, $64 billion of data center projects have been blocked or delayed due to local opposition.

“So not only is Palantir trying to monopolize war technology, it’s now expanding into health technology and trying to dominate AI tech firms to win contracts. And they suspect that Palantir will be the number one beneficiary for the Pax Silica agreement because of the types of technologies they can offer,” Denina said.

She added that despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance. “I think people in the US understand the impacts of the Pax Silica Agreement.”

“To support and facilitate more AI technology, there’s going to be more public funding spent on government contracts to support AI technology. Public spending that could be used towards supporting the local communities,” Denina said, adding that Bagong Alyasang Makabayan (Bayan) US chapter launched the Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network last September was joined by Filipino Americans in the US and other nationalities.

Read: US-wide campaign against Pax Silica launched

Sayeed called on different nations to show resistance against the US whose President is set to come to the Philippines next month.

“I recall reading Joma (Jose Maria Sison). He states that imperialism and feudalism are man-made social phenomena which are to exploit and oppress the people. They are plunderers of both humans and nature,” Sayeed said, adding that critical minerals are key to the industrial military complex as well.

This is why, she said, the US is trying to get hold of the supply chain. She said that the Philippines and Indonesia have critical minerals.

“We must all show up to make sure that he knows Asia. Whether we are in the Philippines or Indonesia or Pakistan or Nepal or India, we have to say, ‘you are not welcome,’” Sayeed said.

“Our resistance has to be fueled by the pain of the people. We fight for our people, we fight for our land, we fight for our destiny. So, that is who we are. And we will not forget.That come 16th of November, when he comes, he will be told you are not welcome across Asia and the Pacific. Let’s make this across Asia and the Pacific, not only the Philippines,” she added. (DAA)

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Mindanao beverage firm workers denounce unequal treatment
content:
Having equal pay is what we are after because we are delivering the same [products].

For months, workers have been demanding an end to a multinational beverage corporation’s alleged unequal treatment of its workforce in Mindanao.

The Samahan ng Manggagawa sa Coca-Cola (SAMACOKE) and Nagkakaisang Manggagawa ng Buong Lohistika at Distribusyon ng Coca-Cola Southern at Central Mindanao (NMLDCC-SCM), both affiliated with the Federation and Cooperation of Cola, Beverage, and Allied Industry Unions (FCCU), have been in negotiations with Coca-Cola Europacific Aboitiz Philippines (CCEAP) for a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) to have equal benefits and wage hikes as their Luzon counterparts.

Edmond*, a Davao City resident and who has been in the company for decades, told Bulatlat that a major concern is the alleged unfair implementation of parameters for workers’ performance incentives. He said that they need to accomplish three certain parameters but this was allegedly not similar to a manufacturing site based in Luzon which requires only one parameter.

“The situation has been reversed. We are the vintage [plant], and we are given parameters that are difficult to achieve,” he said in the vernacular.

Receiving an average P1,500 (US$23.79) of monthly incentive, Edmond said, goes a long way for workers given the increasing prices of basic goods.

Coca-Cola truck drivers in Mindanao, on the other hand, are pushing for an equal reload rate as their Luzon counterparts. Adrian*, who is also a Davao City resident and has been working as a delivery truck driver for the company for more than a decade, said that they get paid P135 (US$2.14) per reload which is too low compared to the supposed reload rate of P265 (US$4.20) in a Coca-Cola manufacturing site in Luzon.

“Having equal pay is what we are after because we are delivering the same [products],” Adrian said in the vernacular.

A reload refers to the second and succeeding delivery of Coca-Cola products to various stores after the first trip. Delivery truck drivers, Adrian said, considered it as their overtime pay.

Both unions also pushed for a P50 (US$0.79) daily wage hike, the same amount allegedly granted to the employees working at the same Luzon-based manufacturing site in 2023. In that year, Edmond said that they were forced to accept the offer of a P40 (US$0.63) increase in daily salary after the provision of other benefits which were also essential for them.

Their last CBA expired in October 2025 but the formal negotiations for a new bargaining agreement started in April this year after it got delayed. As of this writing, both parties have yet to conclude negotiations.

The United Coca-Cola Logistics Employees Association of North Mindanao (UCLEANMINDA-FCCU), covering workers from Misamis Oriental and the cities of Iligan, Butuan, and Zamboanga, is facing a separate issue as the company allegedly refused to bargain.

Jasper Mabuloc, UCLEANMINDA-FCCU president, said that their union was certified as the sole and exclusive bargaining agent (SEBA) of the employees in July. But he said that the company allegedly could not proceed with the negotiation since there was a petition filed by the previous labor union—which allegedly opposed having an election—before the secretary of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE).

The CBA of the previous labor union was also until 2028. “The appeal made by the previous labor union was being used to delay the negotiations,” Mabuloc told Bulatlat in the vernacular. “New union, new CBA.”

Like the NMLDCC-SCM members, the union of Mabuloc also echoed the call for equal reload pay for delivery truck drivers in Mindanao.

Coca-Cola workers have been doing peaceful demonstrations outside their workplace, putting protest banners to voice out their concerns. SAMACOKE is also planning to file a complaint to DOLE after some of their banners were recently taken down by unidentified individuals.

“There should be no disparity because according to what they have said, they nationalized and standardized the implementation of their programs. They should follow,” Edmond said in the vernacular.

Bulatlat reached out to the Coca-Cola company through email on October 18, seeking comments on the alleged disparity of pay and benefits. There was no response as of this posting.

SAMACOKE and NMLDCC-SCM already filed notices of strike. If the company does not have an appropriate response to their demands, Edmond and Mabuloc said that they do not have a choice but to launch a work stoppage. (DAA)

*Real names withheld upon request because of fear of possible reprisal.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Displaced Marawi survivors still long for justice
content:
Marawi displaced survivor Baiminang Madale speaking in the opening of Alongan sa Marawi exhibit. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

More than nine years have passed since the Philippine government declared the “liberation” of Marawi City after the siege that displaced more than 300,000 families. Some of them are now living in different parts of the country, uncertain if they could return.

“We were already familiar with the term bakwit (evacuee/displacement). But the Marawi Siege was different. Before, our bakwit would only last for three days. This time, it feels as though we have been permanently driven out of Marawi,” Baiminang Madale, a displaced Maranao survivor living in Manila, said in the vernacular during the opening of Alongan sa Marawi (One Day in Marawi) exhibit.

The exhibit runs until November 15, 2026, at the Rift Gallery Edsa. It is organized by researchers, journalists, survivors, and advocates to commemorate the ninth year of the city’s so-called liberation. It seeks to provide a visual experience of Marawi from the survivors’ perspective.

“The Maranao, like other tribes and communities, have our own culture, dreams, and lives. Because of the Marawi Siege, we feel as though we have not simply been stripped naked, but forcibly stripped out of our homes that shape our identity,” Madale said. “Marawi is the very heart of the Maranao people. Imagine suddenly losing everything—it is far worse than a nightmare. We never thought something like this could happen to us.”

The Philippine government declared October 17 as Marawi Liberation Day starting in 2017 to mark what it called as a “military victory” against the Islamic State-linked Maute group after a five-month battle.

Madale, who is also part of the board of Ako Bakwit, a group working for the welfare and rights of internally displaced peoples (IDPs), said that there are many more families like hers forced to live in Manila since the siege.

Earlier this year, Bulatlat reported that the displaced families have yet to return to their homes in Marawi. Around 17,000 families or 80,000 individuals are still living in 15 temporary shelters in Marawi and Lanao del Sur, according to Marawi Advocacy Accompaniment.

Read: After 9 years, Marawi displaced families have yet to return to their homes

Under the Marawi Siege Victims Compensation Act of 2022, any owner of a residential, cultural, or commercial structure, and other properties in Marawi’s 24 MAA and eight barangays considered as other affected areas (OAA) is entitled to monetary compensation subject to verification.

Compensation claims, under the law, shall be filed within one year from the date of commencement of the filing (July 4, 2023) to the date of its termination (July 3, 2024).

Read: Group opposes Marawi Siege compensation planned changes

Data from the Marawi Compensation Board (MCB), the government body that awards monetary compensation to eligible claimants, showed that 3,699 claims were resolved from 2023 to June 30, 2026, amounting to P6.154 billion. This is 25.51 percent of the estimated 14,497 total claims to be resolved by the body by 2028.

Mindanao State University Prof. Sorhalia Latip-Yusoph said that the recovery and return process for the survivors are hurdled by a tedious bureaucratic process.

“The government’s requirements for returning are extremely difficult to meet. Sometimes, we do not understand why the process has to be so difficult. Perhaps they want to be strict,” Latip-Yusoph said. “Our fellow Maranaos (in bakwit) are truly the ones who, if we may put it this way, are the reason our hearts continue to ache. Many of them are still living elsewhere. I hope we will not reach the tenth year without being able to return home.”

Task Force Bangon Marawi was a government inter-agency task force group established by former President Rodrigo Duterte in June 2017 to facilitate rehabilitation, recovery, and reconstruction.

However, Madale said that the four stages of the task force’s process did not align with the needs of the IDPs and survivors of the Marawi siege. The process includes registration, mapping, submission of documents, and biometrics. However, most IDPs lack valid identification and their house/land ownership documents– most of the time– are not recognized by the government implementers.

“The process is inhumane. Even application to the Marawi Compensation Board (MCB) is difficult. They even prioritize illegal claimants,” Madale said. “I hope our government finds a dignified way to help us.”

She said that for many displaced survivors living in different parts of the country, going back to Marawi to process compensation means financial resources for the transportation, logistics, and even temporary shelters. MCB does not provide comprehensive compensation and is only limited to lands and titles.

Moro indigenous leader Amirah Lidasan condemned the celebration of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) of the so-called Marawi liberation annually, stressing that there is nothing to celebrate in the widespread human rights violations that transpired during and years after the siege, especially with the bombardment of the city.

“What kind of liberation is this when justice remains denied to the victims and their families, with more than a hundred killed and still missing? Thousands remain barred from returning to their communities, while the government prioritizes tourism infrastructure and a military camp over the people’s right to return,” Lidasan told Bulatlat. “Compensation remains inaccessible to many due to inadequate and uncertain funding. And those responsible such as the AFP were not held accountable for the violations.”

Moro Consensus Group said that such a celebration is not a day of triumph but a “stark annual reminder of unresolved justice, state neglect, and unfulfilled promises.”

The group called on the national government and civil society to establish an independent Truth Commission to investigate the security and political lapses that led to the 2017 siege. They also denounced the pace of processing and payout of the compensation for the survivors.

“Despite thousands of legitimate applications filed by victims who lost their homes and loved ones, the current pace of processing and payout remains agonizingly slow. Thousands of affected families have yet to receive a single peso of their awarded compensation,” Drieza Lininding, chairperson of Moro Consensus Group was quoted in a statement.

What is more appalling for survivors is that there has been no accountability for the siege and the disproportionate military response.

“The military response to flush out the militants relied on months of relentless aerial bombardments and heavy artillery. This indiscriminate approach resulted in the complete devastation of the Most Affected Area (MAA), turning cultural heritage, ancestral homes, and thriving commercial hubs into pulverized rubble,” Lininding said.

Survivors lamented the mainstream portrayal of Marawi as a hotbed of violence and terrorism, dubbing it as a false narrative. Independent journalist Raizza Bello said that the exhibit provides an avenue for the survivors and advocates to see the beauty of the community in Marawi.

“The portrayal of Mindanao is always associated with violence and terrorism, but I witnessed firsthand that Mindanao is not like that. The people there were peaceful and welcoming. Our invitation to the exhibit is to, at least see or take a peak, or experience a day in Marawi in the lens of the displaced or bakwits,” Bello said.

Latip-Yusoph stressed that the city, prior to the siege, was considered as one of the peaceful cities in the Philippines. “We are peace-loving citizens. We love our community, and we welcome our visitors. Yet they portrayed Marawi as a place where you would be in danger if you came here. That was deeply unfair.”

Read: Resolve the continuing Marawi displacement, Marcos Jr. urged

The Philippine government is left with less than two years to process the compensation for survivors before the MCB ceases to exist, since it has a statutory sunset clause that expires in 2028.

There are also more than 3,000 compensation claims that have been transferred to the National Housing Authority (NHA), especially for the properties demolished due to the public infrastructure development under the government’s Marawi Recovery, Rehabilitation, and Reconstruction Program.

“I do not want to think that we have been defeated. The fact that we have this exhibition and gathering means that we have not been defeated. There are still people who care,” Latip-Yusoph said. “In Maranao culture, we have a saying: a single strand of hair may only be strong enough to cut one egg. But when many strands come together, they can stop a large boat.” (RTS, DAA)

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Remembering a driver’s activist route
content:
Elmer Cordero tribute. Photo by Shannia Cabuello/Bulatlat.

This was his kind of honk during protests as he shakes his hand with everyone he encounters. He would happily swing the Piston flag while marching to Mendiola. There, he would gracefully dance to Awit ng Kalayaan (Song of Freedom).

This is also how the jeepney driver and activist Elmer Cordero became a familiar face in the streets. Youth and activists refer to him as “Tatay Elmer.”

Until his last breath, Tatay Elmer devoted himself to the cause despite his limitations.

According to Piston president Mody Floranda, Tatay Elmer had difficulty breathing while he was at the nationwide transport strike on September 29. He was then confined at the Caloocan City Medical Center.

On October 7, he passed away at the age of 78.

For nearly five decades, he has been navigating the routes of Metro Manila as a jeepney driver. Considering his health, he was scheduled to operate at 5:00 pm onwards on the Monumento-Baclaran route.

He became publicly known as one of the Piston 6 who were arrested during the pandemic while staging the “Balik Pasada Protest.” His wife Elvira shared in an interview with Bulatlat that she thought Tatay Elmer would just give some food to his fellow jeepney drivers who had nothing to eat.

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressive solons file bill, resolutions on academic freedom
content:
Photo by John Andrei Rarang, The Staple

Progressive lawmakers under the Makabayan bloc filed House Bill No. 11678, or the Academic Freedom Act on Monday, October 12, a bill seeking to defend academic freedom.

The bill came after recent attacks on academic freedom, such as the suspension of four University of Santo Tomas (UST) student activists for protesting against a campus exhibit by the Philippine Air Force (PAF) and the red-tagging of students and faculty members of the University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS).

In her statement, Kabataan Partylist Rep. Renee Co condemned attempts to silence students who have been at the forefront of the fight for social justice and against corruption, especially since the onset of the flood control scandal.

“Discipline offices and military propaganda must not be used to silence students who are simply asking questions about and wanting to stop state abuse,” the statement read.

The bill, which adopts the 2024 UN Draft Principles for Implementing the Right to Academic Freedom and the 2026 Special Rapporteur Report on Youth Activism, seeks to impose imprisonment and fines on violations of academic freedom, such as militarization of campuses, infiltrating student organizations, filing disciplinary punishments against students who engage in peaceful political dissent, and enacting threats and violence against members of the a

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: 17 Filipino workers in British Columbia fight back against labor trafficking
content:
TORONTO – Seventeen Filipino temporary foreign workers (TFW) in British Columbia (B.C) have come forward to campaign against fraudulent recruitment agency Helping Hands Immigration Services (HHIS) that trafficked them into precarious conditions.

In a press conference held with Migrante BC and Damayan BC, the workers described how they became victims of labor trafficking, including being forced to work long hours, receiving inadequate pay, and experiencing wage theft.

The 17 migrant workers who came from Taiwan, worked over four months in Newfoundland as seasonal workers at a seafood processing plant. After their seasonal employment, they were referred to HHIS recruiters Cherry May Ricafort and Vincent Macalipay to process extension of work permits. According to the workers, the two allegedly took advantage of the situation knowing that they were newcomers and that their work statuses were about to expire.

“We left the Philippines with our hopes and dreams. With the desire for a better future for our families, we took risks working in different countries,” one of the workers said.

In the Canadian immigration system, the Temporary Foreign Worker Program allows Canadian employers to hire foreign workers to fill temporary jobs when qualified Canadians are not available.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Victims’ families hope document dispute won’t delay ICC trial
content:
Victims’ families are hopeful that the trial will continue as the fourth status conference of Rodrigo Duterte’s alleged crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court (ICC) concluded on October 13.

“This is important for us, because we are closely watching for justice to prevail through the ICC,” Dahlia Cuartero, mother of victim Jesus Cuartero, told the media in Filipino. “Justice here in the Philippines is hopeless.”

Duterte attended the status conference for the second time. The ICC Trial Chamber III discussed the preparations, including matters involving witnesses, evidence, disclosures, and the schedule of the first week of trial.

Similar to the previous status conference, ICC Presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked the prosecution to review the relevance of documents to avoid duplication.

The ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said that they have a team of analysts and experts that reviewed each document presented for trial.

The prosecution will also use government data like Philippine National Police (PNP) records and the accomplishment report of the Presidential Communications Operations Office (PCOO) to present the number of killings during Duterte’s presidential term.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Duterte compromises accountability’
content:
Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

The Senate impeachment court granted the prosecution’s manifestation to drop three articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte as it wanted to focus “on what is necessary.” For progressive groups, however, this move undermines calls for accountability.

“Ultimately, the prosecution chose political convenience over true accountability,” said human rights lawyer and former Bayan Muna Party-list Rep. Carlos Isagani Zarate in a statement.

After its earlier manifestation to drop Article III, which accused Sara of bribery, on October 13, the prosecution decided to also drop Article I (alleged misuse of confidential funds) and Article IV (assassination threats). Lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro told the impeachment court that they would only focus on Article II which accuses the Vice President of having alleged unexplained wealth, false statements of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALNs), and prohibited business interests.

Luistro said that the prosecution has presented sufficient evidence on Article II “to stand on its own.”

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, on the other hand, acknowledged the prosecution’s power to withdraw its allegations but she said that the prerogative should not affect how they would counter the accusations against Duterte.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Workers win illegal dismissal case vs Lazada, manpower agencies
content:
In two separate cases, the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) has ruled in favor of platform workers in illegal dismissal cases against manpower companies and leading Southeast Asian e-commerce platform Lazada.

Both cases involve illegal dismissal and non-payment of the 13th month pay.

Josiah David Quising, legal representative of the platform workers in two separate cases, declared that “these victories are important because of the evolving nature of the workplace.”

“We are no longer traditional wherein workers are situated in one physical space, it also extends to the digital space,” Quising told Bulatlat in Filipino.

NLRC is an attached quasi-judicial agency of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) mandated to resolve labor and management disputes involving Filipino workers.

“These winning cases are mere reaffirmation of the rights of platform workers, particularly riders, based on the Supreme Court (decision),” Quising added.

The first case was an illegal dismissal with claims for non-payment of the 13th month pay, cash bond deposit, damages and attorney’s fees by a platform rider against Metro Courier Inc. (MCI) and Lazada.

The NLRC stated that the rider is a “regular employee of respondent Lazada and that he was illegally dismissed by the latter.”

The rider was employed by the manpower services MCI for Lazada. His regular work routine was described

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Six years on, a mother grieves death of son killed in the ‘drug war’
content:
Lorna Carina Pepaño. Screengrab from the Philippine Truth Commission

“For me, justice and healing mean holding accountable those who carried out the killings, the perpetrators, those who gave the orders, and the highest-ranking officials behind the killings.”

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Seeing her son’s body, his blood spilling in the streets, Lorna Carina Pepaño could not cry. That day, on May 18, 2020, her son Christian was shot dead by two unidentified men while buying medicines and coffee for Pepaño.

On the day of the incident, Pepaño ran to the scene of the crime without slippers. Many of the witnesses she talked to said that Christian was begging for his life, telling the perpetrators that he was not the person they were after. The witnesses also heard one of the gunmen saying that Christian was not the target.

Six years later, Pepaño mustered the courage to tell the story of her son during the fourth public truth-telling session organized by the independent Philippine Truth Commission on October 9, 2026.

“All I feel until now is anger,” Pepaño said in Filipino. “Back then, I was shouting, saying words I never thought I could say. Never did I think that my son would be killed that day. I have so many questions but not a single answer.”

author: Alyssa Mae Clarin
title: US-based Filipino migrants protest prolonged ICE detention of slain journalists’ son
content:
Supporters of Mark Mabasa from the Tanggol Migrante Movement and other groups stage a protest in front of Adelanto City Hall after Mabasa's hearing was postponed. Photo by BAYAN USA

Mabasa’s detention is part of a broader pattern of attacks against migrants seeking safety and a better life in the US.

Filipino migrant organizations in the United States rallied behind asylum seeker Mark Mabasa, son of slain Filipino journalist Percival “Lapid” Mabasa, after the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) extended his detention for at least another month.

Mabasa was detained in California as his family sought political asylum in the US following the assassination of his father, veteran journalist Percival “Lapid” Mabasa, on October 3, 2022.

His father was the second journalist killed under the Marcos Jr. administration. His killing remains unresolved, with suspect Gerald Bantag, former chief of the Bureau of Corrections, still at large.

The Mabasa family sought asylum in the US after receiving death threats following the journalist’s killing.

On October 2, a day before the fourth year of his father’s killing, overseas Filipino organizations gathered outside Adelanto ICE Processing Center where Mabasa was being detained to demand his immediate release.

The groups were denied entry to the facility, forcing them to hold the protest outside Adelanto City Hall, five minutes awa

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: People-centered energy urged amid ASEAN Energy Forum
content:
Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of the Kalipunan ng Katutubong Mamamayan ng Pilipinas (Katribu), soeaks during a forum on October 6, 2026. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat

“Energy transition should be an opportunity to develop our self-sufficiency in manufacturing, engineering, and research.”

ASEAN’s energy future is being planned at a forum filled with representatives from corporations, government, banks, and international institutions. Those from grassroots communities are nowhere to be found.

The ASEAN Energy Business Forum was held in Manila from October 5 to 9, bringing more than 1,500 high-level delegates and officials.

“The forum speaks sweetly about innovation, investment, sustainable energy future: identifying projects to fund and profit from,” said Sonny Africa, executive director of think-tank Ibon Foundation, during a parallel conference. “For ordinary people, the essence is not defined by the amount of investments, bankable projects, public-private partnerships, energy companies, and financing but the simplest questions: is the electricity cost lower? Is it more efficient and more accessible?”

The Philippines is assuming the ASEAN chairpersonship this year. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said that the government will use the opportunity to champion “immediate energy security with long-term resilience.”

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressives renew solidarity with Palestinian resistance
content:
MANILA – Progressive formations led by Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), and International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines marched toward the US embassy on the third year since the Al-Aqsa flood. They condemned U.S., Israel and its allies for the continued genocide of Palestine and military aggression on West Asia.

The Al Aqsa Flood refers to the October 7, 2023 attacks led by Hamas that followed Palestine’s long history of resistance against Israel colonial rule and occupation.

For progressives, the Al-Aqsa Flood is not what the west would label as “terrorist attacks” but rather an act of resistance similar to the Philippines, rooted in decades of oppression and colonialism by imperialist nations like the U.S. and Israel. For PPFA, it is the “beacon to our own resistance… It inspires all people struggling for national and social liberation, and therefore, we must support their resistance as if it were our own.”

By the end of the program, progressives burned the flags of U.S. and Israel, calling to stop the genocide, and reaffirming to fight for genuine freedom and the downfall of Imperialism.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Badoy red tags UP Rural High School teacher, community
content:
A teacher and the community of UP Rural High School are the recent targets of red-tagging by former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) spokesperson Lorraine Badoy.

On October 6, Badoy red-tagged UP Rural High School teacher Trist’n Buenaflor. Before this, Badoy, in a series of Facebook posts, also red-tagged faculty members and students of the UP Rural High School after the UP Day Remembrance of Martial Law.

The UP Rural High School released a statement on October 1, condemning the red-tagging by Badoy and a military agent named “Emjay Chico.”

“We believe in developing learners who can think critically and engage with the complex problems confronting Philippine society and affecting their basic rights to education, decent life, and human dignity,” the statement reads. “It is deeply concerning that a legitimate educational activity and those who participated in it have been subjected to red-tagging.”

The University asserts the right to academic freedom: fostering discourse that is open, informed, and grounded in evidence.

For his part, Buenaflor has stood his ground.

“All I can say is that I love teaching, and I deeply value my university. I am not afraid,” Buenaflor told Bulatlat in an interview. “I will continue my studies and continue teaching and serving society. I will keep moving forward.”

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Bukidnon Lumad’s fight for ancestral land remains uncertain
content:
Representatives of the Gulinsao and Maranding clans join a dialogue held at Provincial Tulugan Hall, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, on September 7, 2026. Photo from Bukidnon Provincial IPMR Datu Makayuba Renato Sumbongan’s Facebook page

CAGAYAN DE ORO — After the fifth dialogue aiming to settle the land dispute between Indigenous peoples and a government agency in Barangay Dalwangan, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Lumad are still deprived of their ancestral land.

“They should return the land they borrowed,” Datu Aldren Gulinsao told Bulatlat in the vernacular following the dialogue last month.

Since 2017, the Gulinsao clan belonging to the Talaandig tribe has been reclaiming over 600 hectares of ancestral land, while their relative, the Maranding clan, has been claiming over 400 hectares. These form part of the more than 1,000 hectares of land under the title they obtained during the Philippine Commonwealth owned by their ancestor Maximo Gulinsao.

The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), on the other hand, said the subject land has been a titled property of the Department of Agriculture (DA) since the 1930s.

To assert their rights, in February, a few members of the Gulinsao clan forcibly entered the land, which resulted in the arrest of three individuals.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Festival-themed protest underscores teachers’ economic demands
content:
MANILA – On World Teachers’ Day, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) held a protest near Malacañang Palace billed as “Pistang Protesta: Dagdag Sweldo, Hindi Dagdag Trabaho.”

Teachers from different public and private schools all over Metro Manila, as well as students and supporters marched Padre Noval Street corner España Boulevard toward Mendiola, October 5, 2026.

Carrying bunting flags and surrounded by ice cream carts, protesters called for a reduced and humane workload, allocation of six percent of GDP to education, P5,000 (approximately US$79.68) economic relief allowance and P50,000 (approximately US$796.81) entry-level salary for all teachers.

The current starting basic pay of a Teacher is pegged at P31,705 (approximately US$505.26) while the economic relief allowance is only P2,000 (approximately US$31.87)

Hogier Villarias, secretary general of Alliance of Concerned Teachers NCR, said that their call for salary hike is timely considering the increase in the country’s Gross Domestic Product.

“Our primary call remains a salary increase since our GDP grew by four percent, so we are expecting that wages should also be increased,” said Villarias, who joined the protest along with his fellow teachers from Andres Bonifacio Elementary School.

According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the GDP of the country grew by 4.4 percent in 2025. However

author: Josiah David Quising
title: Family, advocates remember 1987 killing of peasant leader, son
content:
Almost four decades later, they still remember. Friends and family held a memorial and candle lighting activity on October 3 to remember Valeriano Caro and his son who were killed 39 years ago by members of the Composite Reaction Force, a unit of the Regional Special Action Force, under the Cory Aquino administration.

Caro was a peasant leader from Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) and chairperson of the Kahublagan sang Mangunguma sa Isla sang Panay (KAMIPA).

He and his son Rolito were killed in Barangay Galang, Oton, Iloilo on October 3, 1987. The memorial and candle-lighting were held on the roadside near the site where they were killed.

According to his wife in a report published by Amnesty International in 1988, Valeriano and her son were taken by the military at around 9:25 a.m. and were shot by a military officer just 70 meters from their own home.

On his 39th death anniversary, Valeriano’s family recalled his dedication to the plight of farmers in Panay.

“His legacy lives on in the continuing struggle to free farmers from landlessness, from bondage to the land, and from abuses at the hands of the regime,” Panay Alliance Karapatan said in a statement. (DAA)

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Army use of child a violation of int’l humanitarian law’
content:
MANILA – The Philippine Army’s publication of child pictures to pressure a New People’s Army (NPA) member to surrender is a violation of international humanitarian law (IHL), a human rights group said in a statement.

“Posting the child’s name, photograph and location while giving her mother an ultimatum to surrender was not only inhumane and exploitative, it was tantamount to holding the child hostage to compel her mother to do something against her will,” said human rights lawyer Maria Sol Taule, deputy secretary-general of Karapatan, in a statement on October 5.

In a deleted post, the 93rd Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army published photos of a seven-year-old child with personal details under the pretext of a “birthday party” celebration to urge their NPA mother to surrender.

The Philippines is a signatory to the Geneva Conventions and is obligated to follow the rules of war under IHL. “Children shall be the object of special respect and shall be protected against any form of indecent assault. The Parties to the conflict shall provide them with the care and aid they require, whether because of their age or for any other reason,” the Fourth Geneva Convention stated.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Leyte farmer files harassment complaint vs military
content:
By Veronika Barbosa TACLOBAN CITY – A farmer filed a complaint on September 22 with the Commission on Human Rights Regional Office 8 against the Philippine Army’s 93rd Infantry Battalion (IB) due to intimidation against her and her family.

Accompanied by the National Union of People’s Lawyers Eastern Visayas and Katungod Sinirangan Bisayas, Brenda Lagado said that the first incident happened on July 28 in their house in Jaro, Leyte. “We were visited by elements of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. At first, they were just checking in on us but they eventually pressured us to confess that we have connections with the New People’s Army even if we have none.”

In the same month, Lagado said that her 16-year-old cousin was also interrogated by soldiers and alleged military assets.

“He [my cousin] was tending to farm animal when he was approached by seven soldiers and seven other individuals. At first, he was told to wait for a certain Basas who was supposed to talk to him but the latter did not arrive. He was instead confronted by a certain Simon who later grabbed him by the collar, hit him with a piece of chopped wood, and threatened that he will be hanged or electrocuted if he does not cooperate with them.”

Lagado said that his cousin was coerced by at least 14 men to divulge information about certain individuals that the victim does not know about.

title: Labnotes | Ang kontradiksyon ng renewable energy transition sa Pilipinas
content:
The 54MW Pililla Wind Power Project in Pililla, Rizal is operated by Vena Energy. Photo by Chantal Eco

Sa kalagitnaan ng krisis sa klima, ibinibida ng gobyerno at ng mga malalakihang korporasyon ang transition sa renewable energy bilang solusyon — na ang mga solar, wind farm, at iba pa ay susi sa mura’t malinis na enerhiya. Pero habang kinakalbo ang mga kabundukan para itayo ang wind turbines, solar panels, at mga dambuhalang dams, ang bill ng kuryente—palagi pang tumataas!

Ang mga dapat itanong: sino ang may-ari ng mga planta, sinu-sino ang may kontrol ng transmisyon at distribusyon, at para saan ba talaga ang Electric Power Industry Reform Act o EPIRA?

Patuloy ang pagdami ng mga wind at solar farm sa Pilipinas. Noong 2022, 1,530 megawatt (MW) na kuryente ang mula sa solar, at nadoble ito noong 2025 sa 3,003 MW. Umaabot na ngayon sa 3,892 MW (3.9 GW) ang kapasidad mula sa solar, habang ang wind farm o kuryenteng mula sa hangin ay nananatili sa 427 MW lamang.

Sinasabing malinis at mas mura ang kuryenteng nagmumula sa modernong teknolohiyang Renewable Energy (RE) tulad ng solar at wind farm. Ang RE ay teknolohiyang gumagamit ng mga likas na yamang halos di-nauubos tulad ng araw, hangin, at tubig. Mahigit 22 porsyento ng kuryente sa bansa ang galing sa RE — nagmumula ito sa geothermal plants (9.1%), hydroelectric dams (8.7%), solar farm (2.2%), wind farm (1.1%), at iba pang p

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: First Person | Losing a home
content:
Screenshot from Baterno's footage.

Losing CMFR feels a lot like losing a home.

I’ve seen many posts about the closure of the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR), and what it means to Philippine journalism.

But to me, it is deeply personal.

Losing CMFR feels a lot like losing a home.

For over 13 years, the center has been the foundation of everything I’ve built in my career. I joined CMFR simply wanting a job experience that would look good on my resume. Never intended to stay because, as a young adult from the Visayas, the goal was to eventually go mainstream.

But a rocky love-hate relationship with my superior during my early years at the organization challenged me to prove my worth as a staff writer. What started as a constant need to prove myself turned into a genuine appreciation for the work and a deeper understanding of why it mattered.

Before I even realized it, I had become deeply involved in its advocacy — tracking threats and attacks against journalists, assessing news reports on various issues, and conducting comprehensive research on media coverage.

CMFR opened doors for me to travel across the Philippines and the world, expand my network, and meet incredible people. But most importantly, it gave me a space to discover stories that I would often draw inspiration from for my own creative side hustles.

title: Seafarers demand end to US war
content:
eafarer groups along with migrant worker groups held a forum to condemn U.S war against countries, affecting their safe travel at sea. (Photo by Aaron Ernest Cruz/Bulatlat)

The Philippines is not just being exploited from their resources but it is also exposed to the enemies of the U.S.

Condrad Belasa, 28, witnessed military aircraft of Iran and the United States carrying out bombings while working as a seafarer. Although their route was far from the Strait of Hormuz, he said that he still felt afraid.

He recalled an incident on March 11, a month after the U.S started its attack on Iran, when their ship passed through the Green Zone. They saw military aircraft bombing one another in real time. Their crew could do nothing but hope that no missiles or ammunition would hit their ship.

“While we are sailing, we see in the radar that we are being followed by military aircraft. Some of my colleagues said it was a fighter jet but in my personal opinion, I think it was a drone,” Belasa told Bulatlat in an interview.

In his five years of working as a seafarer, this was the first time he found himself caught in the middle of a war. The experience worried him, especially because he has a two-year old child waiting for him to come home.
